Questions for the interviews were sent to participants in advance. In most cases, the interview transcripts were returned to participants for verification. 2. The study by Maggi et al. (2018) investigated fall determinants and home modifications implemented by occupational therapists to prevent falls. It was a quasi-experimental study conducted in Belgium, involving frail adults over 65 years old living at home with a history of falls. Data were collected between 2010 and 2014. The sample size was 1565 participants. The interventions included home modifications and advice provided by occupational therapists, with or without case management. The study had a high risk of bias due to insufficient details on key aspects of the study design. 3. The study by Norin et al. (2017) examined housing accessibility and its associations with participation among older adults living with long-standing spinal cord injuries in Sweden. It was a cross-sectional study conducted in Lund, Sweden, involving adults aged 50 years or older with spinal cord injuries lasting at least 10 years. The study aimed to describe the housing situation and participation aspects of these individuals, considering the severity of their spinal cord injuries, and to explore the association between objective housing accessibility and participation. The study had a high risk of bias due to a lack of details on key aspects of the study design. 4. The study by Petersson et al. (2008) assessed the impact of home modification services on the ability to perform everyday activities for people aging with disabilities. It was a quasi-experimental pre-post test study conducted in Sweden, involving adults aged 40 years or older with disabilities who requested home modifications. Data were collected between 2002 and 2005. Participants scheduled for home modifications within four weeks were allocated to the intervention group, while those waiting for their applications to be processed were placed in the comparison group. Common modifications included shower installations, ramps, and automatic door openers. The intervention group experienced decreased difficulties and increased safety in bathroom use and entering/exiting the home. However, no significant changes were observed in the comparison group. The study had limitations, including a small sample size, urban living samples, and psychometric limitations in the assessment tools. 5. The study by Petersson et al. (2009) investigated longitudinal changes in everyday life after home modifications for people aging with disabilities. It was a quasi-experimental pre-post test study conducted in Sweden, involving adults aged 40 years or older with disabilities who requested home modifications. Data were collected between 2002 and 2005. Participants in the intervention group received home modifications, while the comparison group did not. Common modifications included showers, ramps, and automatic door openers. The intervention group showed improvements in safety and reduced difficulties in activities of daily living, while no effects were observed in the comparison group. The study had limitations, including a small sample size, high dropout rates, and urban living samples that may not be generalizable. 6. The study by Stark (2004) evaluated the impact of removing environmental barriers in the homes of older adults with disabilities on occupational performance. It was a non-randomized pre-post study conducted in the USA, involving low-income older adults with functional impairments who required environmental modifications. Data were collected between 1999 and 2000. Participants received an average of five home modifications, including handrails, grab bars, and ramps. Less common modifications included bed rails, widened doorways, and relocated laundry facilities. The interventions were limited to compensatory strategies, and no remedial interventions were provided. The study used the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) to assess outcomes. The study had limitations, including a small sample size, lack of a control group, and a population that was not representative of the general older adult population with disabilities. 7. The study by Slaug et al. (2017) examined the short-term costs and long-term gains of improved housing accessibility for older people in Sweden and Germany. It was a cross-sectional study conducted between 2002 and 2003, involving adults aged 80-89 years from the ENABLE-AGE survey. The study aimed to estimate the potential impact of improved housing accessibility on instrumental activities of daily living (I-ADL), home service usage, and related costs. The sample size included 397 participants in Sweden and 450 in Germany at baseline. The study found that improved housing accessibility could maintain or improve the health of the aging population. However, there was a moderate risk of bias due to insufficient information on some aspects of the study design. 8. The study by Stineman et al. (2007) investigated the relationship between home accessibility features and activities of daily living (ADL) in adults with disabilities in the USA. It was a cross-sectional survey study using data from the National Health Interview Survey on Disability (NHIS-D). Phase I data were collected between 1994 and 1997, and Phase II data were collected 206 to 722 days later. The sample size included 25,805 participants in Phase II. The study found that self-perceived environmental barriers, such as lack of ramps or wide doorways, were associated with difficulties in ADL. The study had limitations, including a focus on physical limitations and potential errors from non-response bias in the original survey. 9. The study by Tchalla et al. (2012) evaluated the efficacy of simple home-based technologies combined with a monitoring assistive center in reducing falls among frail elderly individuals in France. It was a longitudinal cohort pilot study conducted between July 2009 and June 2010. Participants received interventions such as light paths and tele-assistance services, while the control group did not receive any intervention. The study found that the interventions improved visibility and awareness of the environment, reducing the rate of falls. However, the study had limitations, including potential recall bias and a small sample size. 10. The study by Tongsiri et al. (2017) described the results and lessons learned from implementing a home modification program for individuals with physical disabilities in Thailand. It was a quasi-experimental study conducted in 2013, involving 43 participants. The program involved a multidisciplinary team of medical and non-medical practitioners and volunteers to address functional difficulties through home modifications. The study found improvements in participants' ability to perform daily activities after modifications. However, there was a high risk of bias due to insufficient details on key aspects of the study design.
